category: Topic, reference, respect, role, and capacity

entries.ipa: /əˈbaʊt/ · casual clipped form /ˈbaʊt/ ('bout) · the stressed second syllable never reduces; only the unstressed first one drops
entries.type: simple (historically a fusion of Old English on + būtan "outside") — also an adverb (there was nobody about), a degree modifier (about forty), and a verb particle (bring it about, come about)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (about starting the job), or a wh-clause (about what happened, about whether to go, about how it works) — never a bare that-clause (✗ I told her about that the meeting moved). To carry a that-clause you must insert a noun: about the fact that she left. As an adverb or particle it takes no object at all.
entries.pattern: [verb] about [noun phrase] / [noun] about [noun phrase] / [adjective] about [noun phrase] / stranded: the thing I told you about / fronted and formal: the matter about which we spoke
entries.contrast: Against on, about is the general, conversational topic word and on is the scholarly one: a book about bees is for anyone, a book on bees is a treatise. On also implies sustained, organized treatment, which is why you can give a lecture on Keats but only a quick word about your weekend. Against over, about is neutral where over implies a fight. The "scattered here and there" sense (papers lying about the room) is British; American English says around, and British round is not an American option. Cross-class test — the object: we talked about the merger is the preposition (object the merger); there was nobody about and about forty people are adverbs with nothing after them to govern; bring it about is a particle, where the object it belongs to bring; and be about to is a fixed idiom in which about governs nothing and cannot be moved or stranded.
entries.meaning: The most useful preposition in this file and the default for every job the others do. It is also one of the most polysemous words in English, and only the first three senses are topic senses. 1. Subject matter — what a book, conversation, film, or complaint is on. 2. The target of a feeling or attitude — what the emotion is pointed at. 3. The essential point or nature of something, usually in a corrective sentence. 4. Occupied with, engaged in — a limited, slightly old-fashioned use. 5. Here and there within an area — chiefly British; American English says around. 6. Not a preposition — the degree modifier "approximately," which has no object. 7. Not a preposition — the adverb and the verb particle, and the frozen idiom be about to.
examples: It's a documentary about two brothers who rebuilt a lighthouse.
She wouldn't tell me anything about the interview.
He's still upset about the parking ticket.
I'm excited about starting the new job.
This isn't about the money — it's about being taken seriously.
Good teaching is about knowing when to stay quiet.
Go about your business and don't stare.
While you're about it, could you refill the ice tray?
There were toys lying about the living room.
He spent the morning wandering about the museum.
There were about forty people in the room.
We got there about nine.
The trip takes about an hour and a half.
There was nobody about when we pulled in.
Nobody knows how the change came about.
She was about to leave when the phone rang.

entries.ipa: /kənˈsɜrnɪŋ/ · no weak form — like the other participial prepositions (regarding, respecting, touching) it keeps its stressed second syllable in every register; only the prefix vowel reduces, to /kən-/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (concerning failing to file on time), or a fused wh-nominal (concerning who authorized the transfer) — never a finite that-clause. ✗ Concerning that he resigned is impossible; write concerning his resignation or concerning the fact that he resigned.
entries.pattern: [clause] concerning [noun phrase] / Concerning [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Regarding is the neutral business default; concerning is heavier and gravitates toward inquiries, complaints, allegations, and official correspondence. Cross-class test — the object: the preposition always has one and never follows a linking verb (a complaint concerning the instructor), while the modern adjective meaning "worrying" has no object and sits happily after is (that's concerning, a concerning trend). If you can drop very in front of it, you have the adjective.
entries.meaning: Introduces the matter an official communication is about. Unlike the participial prepositions of cause (considering, given), it has lost every trace of its verb: no subject is implied and nothing is doing any concerning. 1. The subject of an inquiry, complaint, or official communication — the core sense, and the reason the word survives in correspondence at all. 2. The matter a document, rule, or statute covers or conspicuously fails to cover, very common after silent, vague, no documentation, no provision. 3. Not a preposition — the modern adjective meaning "worrying," which governs nothing, follows a linking verb freely, and takes degree modifiers the preposition cannot.
examples: I'm writing concerning the invoice dated March 4.
The committee received two complaints concerning the same instructor.
Concerning your request for an extension, the deadline is fixed by statute.
The statute is silent concerning leases signed before 1998.
There is no documentation concerning who authorized the transfer.
She refused to answer questions concerning her time at the agency.
The trend in the third quarter is concerning.
Two of the lab values came back concerning enough to repeat.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈreɪ/ · also /ɪn ˈri/ · no weak form — the re carries the stress and keeps its full vowel, and the Latin in is not the reduced English in of in a minute
entries.complement: a noun phrase, almost always a proper name or the name of an estate, matter, or proceeding. No gerund, and no clause of any kind — not a that-clause and not a wh-nominal.
entries.pattern: In re [noun phrase] — as a case caption, docket heading, or file label
entries.contrast: Re is the clipped commercial descendant of this phrase and belongs in memos, not pleadings. In re survives in American practice mainly to caption a matter that has no opposing party — a bankruptcy, an estate, a juvenile proceeding — where there is no v. to write.
variants: sub nom. (short for sub nomine, "under the name of") — the companion caption tag used when the same matter was decided below under a different name
In the Matter of (the English rendering, which some state courts prefer in full)
entries.meaning: Latin for "in the matter of," and used for exactly that. Outside case captions it is affected.
examples: In re Gault remains the foundational juvenile due-process case.
The clerk filed it under In re Estate of Margaret Voss.
In re Marriage of Hoffman was decided the following term.
Counsel cited three bankruptcy opinions, all captioned in re the same debtor.
The docket entry read simply In re Grand Jury Subpoena.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈmætər əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈmætər ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in the matter of who pays for repairs); never a finite that-clause (✗ in the matter of that the funds are missing).
entries.pattern: In the matter of [noun phrase] / [clause] in the matter of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The English of in re, and the form you want when you are writing for readers rather than for a docket. Against on the subject of, it is heavier and implies a proceeding, a decision, or a formal position rather than a conversation.
entries.meaning: Names the business at hand with deliberate ceremony. In running prose it signals that something official is being disposed of.
examples: In the matter of the disputed easement, the court found for the defendant.
The board has reached no conclusion in the matter of the missing funds.
In the matter of your suspension, you may request a hearing within ten days.
She was called to testify in the matter of the 2019 audit.
In the matter of who pays for repairs, the lease is unambiguous.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈsʌbdʒɪkt əv/ · weak /ɑn ðə ˈsʌbdʒɪkt ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (on the subject of who pays); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: On the subject of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] on the subject of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Fronted, it works like speaking of — a bridge from what was just said. Mid-sentence it is simply an expanded on, and the expansion buys you the ability to attach a long noun phrase without ambiguity: a chapter on the subject of nineteenth-century tariffs cannot be misread the way a chapter on nineteenth-century tariffs occasionally can.
variants: on the topic of (interchangeable)
on the question of (leans toward a matter genuinely in dispute)
on the matter of (heavier, and drifting toward in the matter of)
entries.meaning: Announces the topic explicitly, either to open it or to change to it.
examples: On the subject of money, we should talk before the meeting.
He has written three books on the subject of memory.
The senator has been notably quiet on the subject of the pipeline.
On the subject of who pays for the venue, nothing has been decided.
She had strong opinions on the subject of letting children lose at games.
On the subject of dinner — is anyone actually cooking?

entries.ipa: /ˈoʊvər/ · no weak form — unlike the one-syllable prepositions around it, over keeps its stress and its full first vowel even in fast speech; the clipped o'er /ɔr/ is poetic only
entries.type: simple — also an adverb and adjective (the meeting was over), a verb particle (hand it over, think it over), and a directional adverb (come over)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (sued over failing to disclose the defect), or a fused wh-nominal in the dispute sense (a fight over who gets the house, disagreement over whether to appeal) — never a finite that-clause (✗ they argued over that the rent was late → they argued over the late rent). As an adverb or particle it takes no object at all, which is the test that separates the two.
entries.pattern: [noun of conflict] over [noun phrase] / [verb of conflict, distress, or deliberation] over [noun phrase] / over [wh-nominal] / stranded: what exactly are they fighting over?
entries.contrast: Against about, over adds friction: you talk about the merger but you fight over it, and a discussion about the budget and a dispute over the budget differ in temperature, not in subject. Against on, which frames a topic for study, over frames it for combat. Against in connection with, over names the cause outright where that phrase deliberately declines to. Cross-class test — the object: they argued over the bill is the preposition (object the bill); the argument was over is the adjective, with nothing after it; hand it over is a particle, where the object it belongs to hand and over governs nothing; and come over sometime is a bare directional adverb. Senses treated elsewhere: this entry covers only the topic senses — the spatial ("above," "across"), covering, authority, medium, and "more than" senses are in movement and direction, and the "spanning a period" sense (over the weekend) is in time.
entries.meaning: The preposition of things people quarrel about. Whenever the head noun or verb involves conflict, grief, deliberation, or consequence, English reaches for over rather than about — and the choice is idiomatic rather than logical, so it has to be learned verb by verb. 1. The matter two parties are fighting about, after the nouns argument, dispute, fight, quarrel, row, battle, standoff, litigation, deadlock and the verbs argue, fight, quarrel, clash, split, fall out, deadlock, haggle. 2. The trigger of a strong reaction — a resignation, a lawsuit, an arrest, a firing. 3. The subject of worry, grief, fuss, or slow deliberation, after agonize, brood, fret, fuss, obsess, pore, mull, labor, grieve, cry. 4. Not a preposition — the adverb, adjective, and verb particle, which take no object.
examples: The strike began as an argument over scheduling software.
Two families have been in court over forty feet of shoreline.
Congress deadlocked over the disaster funding bill.
There is still disagreement over who signs the release.
The deputy director resigned over the handling of the complaint.
The city was sued over the condition of the pumping station.
Two contractors were charged over the falsified inspection reports.
He's still beating himself up over one bad quarter.
She pored over the lease for the better part of an hour.
Nobody is going to cry over a broken plate.
The meeting was over by four.
He handed over the keys without a word.
Come over whenever you like.

entries.ipa: /ri/ · also /reɪ/ · no weak form — it is a stressed monosyllable on the rare occasions it is read aloud
entries.type: simple (a clipping of Latin in re)
entries.register: business and legal shorthand — written only, and effectively never spoken in running prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase. No gerund, and no clause of any kind; a pronoun object is possible only in the fixed heading Re: yours of the 14th and is otherwise avoided.
entries.pattern: Re: [noun phrase] — as a memo or letter heading / re [noun phrase] — inside a docket line or file label
entries.contrast: Re is not an abbreviation of regarding or of reference, so it takes no period. In a heading it is conventionally followed by a colon; inside a sentence it looks like jargon, and regarding or about is better. Not to be confused with the prefix re- of rewrite and reissue, which is bound and hyphenated where it is written at all, or with the re of do re mi, which is a different word entirely — the preposition is free-standing and takes neither hyphen nor period.
entries.meaning: The subject line of the English language. It labels what a document is about, and it does not belong in the body of one. 1. As a heading, followed by a colon — the overwhelmingly commoner use, and the only one that is above criticism. 2. Inside running text or a file label — jargon, and worth replacing with about or regarding.
examples: Re: Termination of Lease, 41 Colfax Avenue.
The memo was headed Re: Q3 headcount and ran to nine pages.
Re: your voicemail — the shipment left Tuesday.
Please reply to my note re the Thursday deposition.
Every filing in the folder was marked re the same policy number.
He sent one line re the Henderson closing and nothing since.

entries.ipa: /rɪˈɡɑrdɪŋ/ · no weak form — the stress on -gard- is fixed, and the -ing may go /-ɪn/ in casual speech but the vowel of the stressed syllable never reduces
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word in American business writing
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (regarding filing after the deadline), or a fused wh-nominal (regarding what the auditors found, regarding whether to appeal) — never a finite that-clause (✗ regarding that the auditors found an error → regarding the auditors' finding).
entries.pattern: [clause] regarding [noun phrase] / Regarding [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The shortest member of the regard family and the only one that is a single word — prefer it to with regard to, in regard to, and as regards, which say the same thing in three words. There is no s: regardings and as regarding are not English, and regarding to is an error. Cross-class test — the subject: the preposition implies no subject and can open a sentence with nothing to attach to (Regarding your application, a decision is due Friday); the identically spelled present participle of the verb regard must share its subject with the main clause (Regarding the painting closely, she noticed the repair — she is doing the regarding). If the -ing word has an agent, it is the participle.
entries.meaning: The neutral formal word for "about." It has no attitude, no implication of complaint, and no legal flavor, which is what makes it the safe default in correspondence. 1. Concerning — the plain topic sense. 2. Attaching a topic to a noun or adjective of communication, after question, silence, guidance, correspondence, and after cagey, evasive, forthcoming, explicit. 3. With a fused wh-nominal, where the topic is itself an open question.
examples: Regarding your application, we expect to decide by the fifteenth.
I have a question regarding the deductible.
The email said nothing regarding payment.
Several parents have written regarding the change to the bus route.
She was cagey regarding her plans after graduation.
The department has issued no guidance regarding remote work.
Regarding who should attend, that's the director's call.
Regarding what the auditors found, nobody will say anything on the record.

entries.ipa: /rɪˈspɛktɪŋ/ · no weak form — identical in this respect to the noun phrase with respect to, where respect also keeps its full stressed vowel while the words around it reduce
entries.register: formal and dated; still productive in legal drafting
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (respecting selling the timber); a fused wh-nominal is grammatical but rare (respecting who may vote); never a finite that-clause (✗ respecting that the trust was funded).
entries.pattern: [clause] respecting [noun phrase] / Respecting [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The reason this word is fading is that it collides head-on with the participle of the verb respect. A law respecting religion means "a law about religion" in the First Amendment and "a law that shows deference to religion" in ordinary modern reading — and nothing in the sentence disambiguates. Use regarding or about unless you are quoting.
entries.meaning: The eighteenth-century sibling of regarding, preserved mostly by constitutional and statutory text. 1. Concerning, about — the prepositional sense. 2. Not a preposition — the present participle of the verb respect, which is the collision that is killing the word; the participle has a subject and the preposition does not.
examples: Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion.
The trustee has broad discretion respecting the sale of estate property.
Rules respecting the admission of new members are set out in Article IV.
He would say nothing respecting the terms of the settlement.
The manual is vague respecting overtime.
Respecting her wishes, the family held no service.
A statute respecting tribal sovereignty may be one that concerns it or one that defers to it, and the sentence will not tell you which.

entries.ipa: /ˈtʌtʃɪŋ/ · no weak form — stress falls on the first syllable and stays there
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; a fused wh-nominal is possible in older text (touching what was owed him); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] touching [noun phrase] / Touching [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Identical in meaning to concerning and three hundred years older in feel. It also has an unrelated adjective twin meaning "moving" (a touching tribute), so a modern reader hits touching the estate and stalls.
variants: touching on
touching upon (these are the living verb-plus-particle construction — the report touches on funding — and a different structure from the preposition, which needs no on)
entries.meaning: The Renaissance word for "concerning," now confined to deliberate period style, older legal instruments, and church documents. 1. Concerning — the prepositional sense. 2. Not a preposition — the adjective meaning "moving" and the participle of the verb touch; neither governs a topic, and the adjective governs nothing at all.
examples: Touching the matter of the boundary wall, the parties are agreed.
He left instructions touching the disposal of his library.
Touching your inquiry of the tenth, I can say little.
There is an ancient canon touching the fitness of candidates.
She wrote at length touching her father's debts.
It was a touching tribute, and nobody had expected it.
He read the whole letter without touching the envelope again.

entries.ipa: /əˈnɛnt/ · no weak form — the stressed second syllable keeps its full vowel and only the unstressed a- reduces
entries.register: archaic; alive in Scots law and in deliberately antique or jocular writing
entries.complement: noun phrase only. A gerund is grammatical but unidiomatic, and no clause of any kind will go here — not a that-clause and not a wh-nominal.
entries.pattern: [clause] anent [noun phrase] / Anent [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Means precisely concerning and adds nothing but age. Readers who do not know it will assume you meant ancient or mistyped something, which is a good reason to leave it alone outside Scotland.
entries.meaning: A survival from Middle English, kept in circulation by Scottish legal usage and by writers reaching for a period effect.
examples: Anent the disposition of the estate, the sheriff has issued no interlocutor.
He wrote a long, cranky letter to the editor anent the new parking scheme.
There is an old rule anent the grazing of sheep on common land.
Anent your question, I have consulted the minutes.
The pamphlet sets out the author's views anent the theater.

entries.ipa: /ˌæprəˈpoʊ əv/ · weak /ˌæprəˈpoʊ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (apropos of what you just said); never a finite that-clause. As an adjective (sense 3) it takes no complement at all.
entries.pattern: Apropos of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause], apropos of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Not a general synonym for about. It means "prompted by" or "arising out of," so it needs something already on the table to arise from. It is also an adjective meaning "apt" (an apropos remark), where it takes no object at all.
variants: à propos of (with the accent; older and now uncommon in American text)
bare apropos used directly as a preposition (apropos your email) — widespread, but conservative usage guides still want the of
entries.meaning: Marks a remark as occasioned by something just mentioned. Its single most common appearance in American English is the fixed phrase apropos of nothing, which announces the opposite — a remark with no connection to anything. 1. Prompted by, arising out of. 2. The fixed phrase apropos of nothing. 3. As an adjective — no object, and no of.
examples: Apropos of your point about staffing, we lost two nurses last month.
She mentioned, apropos of the renovation, that the wiring was original.
Apropos of nothing, my brother once met him in an airport.
He announced, apropos of nothing at all, that he was learning Portuguese.
Her question was brief and entirely apropos.
The timing of the announcement was hardly apropos.

entries.ipa: /æz kənˈsɜrnz/ · weak /əz kənˈsɜrnz/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-clause; never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: As concerns [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] as concerns [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Built exactly like as regards, with a verb agreeing with an implied subject, which is why the -s is fixed: as concern is an error, and there is no as concerns to. Rarer and stiffer than as regards; regarding beats both.
entries.meaning: Frames a topic in formal writing, usually to mark a shift to one part of a larger question.
examples: As concerns the second charge, the evidence is thin.
The policy is unchanged as concerns part-time employees.
As concerns funding, the department has made no commitment.
Nothing in the agreement is ambiguous as concerns termination.
As concerns what happens after the merger, no one will say.

entries.ipa: /æz ˈfɔr/ · weak /əz fɚ/, also written /əz fər/
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun (as for me, as for them — never ✗ as for I), gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (as for what he said afterward); never a finite that-clause (✗ as for that he was late).
entries.pattern: As for [noun phrase], [clause]. — essentially always sentence-initial; it cannot be stranded and it does not sit comfortably at the end of a sentence.
entries.contrast: As for switches to a topic already in play, usually one of several items, and very often signals that the new item will fare worse than the last (As for the rest of you...). As to raises a matter for consideration and can sit anywhere in the sentence. With regard to and as regards are neutral framing devices with no contrastive charge at all.
entries.meaning: The English topic-switch marker. It picks one item out of a set under discussion and turns to it.
examples: The tomatoes did well. As for the peppers, something ate them.
As for me, I'd rather drive.
She got a raise and a corner office. As for her old team, they were reassigned.
As for paying the whole thing up front, that isn't happening.
The engine is fine. As for the transmission, I'd get a second opinion.
As for what he said afterward, I'd rather not repeat it.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.ipa: /æz ˈpɜr/ · weak /əz pɚ/
entries.type: complex (English as + Latin per "through, by," pressed into commercial service)
entries.register: business and commercial; long and loudly disliked by usage guides
entries.complement: noun phrase only — a document, an instruction, a conversation, or a published standard. No gerund, no wh-nominal, and never a finite clause: ✗ as per you asked → as per your request, or better, as you asked.
entries.pattern: As per [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] as per [noun phrase] / fixed: as per usual
entries.contrast: As per claims conformity with a prior instruction, which is what separates it from the rest of this family: in reference to and with reference to merely name a document, while as per asserts that the document was followed. It is redundant on its face — per by itself already means "in accordance with" — which is why editors reduce it to per, under, following, or as you asked. Do not confuse it with distributive per (sixty miles per hour, twelve dollars per person), which is a different word doing arithmetic and is perfectly respectable.
variants: per (per your email, per the contract) — shorter, and now the commoner form in American business writing
as per usual (a jocular or dialectal substitute for as usual)
entries.meaning: The invoice-and-work-order preposition. It survives because it sounds official, and it survives in spite of a century of hostility from every American usage authority that has bothered to mention it. 1. In accordance with a stated instruction, document, or standard — the object is the thing that was followed. 2. The fixed phrase as per usual, jocular or dialectal, and not a use of sense 1 since nothing is being conformed to.
examples: As per your instructions, the shipment was split across two pallets.
The invoice was issued as per the terms of the master agreement.
Overtime is calculated as per Section 14 of the handbook.
As per our conversation Tuesday, I've attached the revised scope.
The samples were stored as per the manufacturer's specification.
He showed up twenty minutes late, as per usual.
The printer jammed on the first page, as per usual.

entries.ipa: /æz rɪˈɡɑrdz/ · weak /əz rɪˈɡɑrdz/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a wh-clause; never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: As regards [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] as regards [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: As regards to is an error — a blend of as regards and with regard to. Choose one or the other. And note that this is the one place in the family where an s is correct: regards here is the verb regard agreeing with an implied subject ("as it regards"), not the plural of the noun. Compare with regard to, where the s is always wrong.
variants: as respects (rare, legal drafting)
entries.meaning: A formal, slightly British-flavored way to introduce a topic. Every American editor will shorten it to regarding or about.
examples: As regards the deposit, the tenant has thirty days to dispute it.
The rules are stricter as regards imported produce.
As regards staffing, nothing changes until January.
He was evasive as regards the source of the funds.
As regards whether the flight is refundable, read the fare rules.

entries.ipa: /æz ˈtu/ · weak /əz tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (as to paying the balance), or a wh-clause including one headed by whether (as to whether the deal closes) — never a finite that-clause (✗ no doubt as to that the roof will fail) and never a bare infinitive (✗ as to pay the balance). The to here is a preposition, which is why a verb after it takes -ing; the one construction that looks like an exception is the infinitival indirect question, where the infinitive belongs to the wh-word and not to as to: no guidance as to how to proceed, undecided as to whether to appeal.
entries.pattern: [noun of doubt or dispute] as to [wh-clause] / [clause] as to [noun phrase] / As to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: After a verb, as to is usually deadweight: they disagreed as to how it happened is better as they disagreed about how it happened. After an abstract noun it earns its place, because bare of would change the meaning or fail outright — no evidence as to motive is standard, questions as to whether is standard, and doubt of whether is not English. Against as for, as to does not switch topics; it opens a question.
entries.meaning: The standard bridge from a noun of uncertainty to an indirect question. That is the job it does that no other member of this family does as cleanly. 1. Attaching a wh- or whether-clause to a noun of doubt, question, or dispute. 2. Concerning, with an ordinary noun phrase or a gerund. 3. Fronted, as a topic marker — an older use, now overlapping with as for.
examples: There is real doubt as to whether the roof will last the winter.
She gave no hint as to where she'd been.
The report reaches no conclusion as to who ordered the transfer.
The manual gives no guidance as to how to reset the controller.
The parties remain apart as to damages.
He was questioned as to his whereabouts on the night of the fire.
The lease says nothing as to subletting the garage.
As to the second proposal, the board took no action.
As to money, we'll discuss that when the work is done.

entries.ipa: /ɪn kəˈnɛkʃən wɪθ/ · weak /ɪn kəˈnɛkʃən wəθ/ · also /wɪð/, /wəð/ before a vowel
entries.register: formal; a fixture of police statements, journalism, and securities filings
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in connection with relocating), or a fused wh-nominal (in connection with what happened that night); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in connection with [noun phrase] / In connection with [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: In crime reporting this is a deliberate hedge — arrested in connection with the robbery asserts a link without asserting guilt, which arrested for the robbery would. Do not treat the two as interchangeable; the substitution is a defamation problem, not a style choice.
entries.meaning: States that something is linked to a matter without specifying how. That vagueness is the point, both in journalism and in contracts. 1. Linked to an event, with no claim about how — the police department's and the reporter's hedge. 2. Arising out of or in the course of a transaction — the drafter's catch-all, written broadly on purpose so that nothing touching the deal escapes the clause. 3. Loosely causal, where the writer declines to say "because of."
examples: Two men were detained in connection with the warehouse fire.
She was interviewed in connection with an ongoing investigation.
No charges have been filed in connection with the incident.
The firm disclosed fees paid in connection with the offering.
All expenses incurred in connection with relocating will be reimbursed.
The indemnity covers any claim in connection with the services.
He resigned in connection with the audit findings, though the company said otherwise.
Two supervisors were reassigned in connection with the missing inventory.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈrɛf(ə)rəns tu/ · weak /ɪn ˈrɛfrəns tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in reference to what you asked on Tuesday); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: In reference to [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in reference to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: With reference to is the commoner of the pair in American business writing and means exactly the same thing. Neither takes an s — in references to is a different construction entirely (plural mentions), and in regards to is the analogous error one family over. Both are stiff; regarding or about is nearly always better.
entries.meaning: Points back to a document, a message, or a prior communication. It is at its most natural when there really is a document being referred to.
examples: In reference to your letter of June 2, the policy lapsed in April.
I'm calling in reference to an invoice we received twice.
The clause is ambiguous in reference to renewal.
In reference to the earlier discussion, the figures have since changed.
She said nothing in reference to the missed deadline.

entries.ipa: /ɪn rɪˈɡɑrd tu/ · weak /ɪn rɪˈɡɑrd tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in regard to who signs the checks); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: In regard to [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in regard to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: In regards to is an error, and it is one of the most frequent in American office email. The noun is regard, singular. See with regard to for the full rule and the one exception.
variants: with regard to (the same phrase with a different opening preposition, and slightly more common in American prose)
entries.meaning: A three-word about, indistinguishable in meaning from with regard to.
examples: In regard to your question, the deadline has not moved.
The two departments have different policies in regard to travel.
In regard to the second invoice, we've issued a credit.
He had no authority in regard to hiring.
Nothing has been decided in regard to next year's budget.

entries.ipa: /ɪn rɪˈleɪʃən tu/ · weak /ɪn rɪˈleɪʃən tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in relation to what the policy covers); never a finite that-clause. In the comparative sense (2) the object must be a noun phrase — a gerund will not go there.
entries.pattern: [clause] in relation to [noun phrase] / In relation to [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The only member of this family that also carries a genuine comparative sense — small in relation to the whole measures one thing against another, which with regard to and as regards cannot do. When you mean nothing but "about," the shorter word is better; when you mean "measured against," this is the right phrase and vis-à-vis is its fancier twin.
entries.meaning: 1. Concerning, with respect to. 2. Compared with, measured against, in proportion to — and here the object must be a noun phrase.
examples: The committee has no jurisdiction in relation to private employers.
In relation to the shipping delay, we've waived the fee.
The report says nothing in relation to who approved the overtime.
The engine is enormous in relation to the size of the boat.
Wages have barely moved in relation to rent.
Their sample is tiny in relation to the population they claim to describe.
The debt looks manageable in relation to the company's cash on hand.

entries.ipa: /ɪn rɪˈspɛkt əv/ · weak /ɪn rɪˈspɛkt ə/
entries.register: formal and legal; British and Commonwealth-leaning
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; never a finite clause of any kind. In its home register — insurance, tax, and contract drafting — the object is almost always a bare noun naming a liability, a period, an asset, or a class of loss.
entries.pattern: [clause] in respect of [noun phrase] / In respect of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: American writers should use with respect to. In respect of reads as British or as consciously legal, and it is the form that turns up in insurance policies, tax notices, and contracts drafted outside the United States. Do not confuse either with out of respect for, which is about deference, not topic.
variants: in respect to (American, but far less common than with respect to)
with respect to (the standard American form)
entries.meaning: Identifies the thing a right, payment, liability, or rule applies to. 1. The subject a right, claim, payment, or liability attaches to. 2. The period or unit a charge is computed for — the tax-and-insurance use, and the one with no short American equivalent, where for is usually the answer. 3. Concerning, as regards — the plain topic use, which American writers should render with respect to.
examples: No claim may be made in respect of damage caused by ordinary wear.
The company accepted liability in respect of the two damaged pallets.
Nothing is owed in respect of the canceled order.
Tax is payable in respect of the year ending April 5.
A premium is charged in respect of each insured vehicle.
In respect of the remaining units, completion is scheduled for June.
The policy is silent in respect of flood.

entries.ipa: /ɑn ðə ˈskɔr əv/ · weak /ɑn ðə ˈskɔr ə/
entries.register: formal and dated; only the fixed on that score is still ordinary American English
entries.complement: a noun phrase, characteristically a bare abstract noun naming a dimension of judgment — cost, safety, health, taste, proportion. A gerund is grammatical but stiff (on the score of having failed to file), and no clause of any kind will go here.
entries.pattern: [clause] on the score of [noun phrase] / On the score of [noun phrase], [clause] / fixed: on that score, on this score
entries.contrast: Two readings sit inside the phrase, and they belong to different files. As a topic limiter it means "as regards" — no complaints on the score of comfort — and as a reason phrase it means "on the grounds of," where it overlaps on the grounds of and on account of. The test is what the object names: a dimension gives you the topic sense, a motive the causal one. Nothing to do with music or with keeping score in a game, though the metaphor did start as a tally scratched on a tavern beam.
variants: on that score, on this score — anaphoric, fully alive, and the only forms most Americans ever write (you can set your mind at rest on that score)
entries.meaning: Restricts a judgment to one dimension, the way as regards does, with a Victorian accent. Modern American writing keeps the anaphoric form and drops the rest.
examples: The proposal was rejected on the score of cost alone.
Nobody has complained on the score of noise.
On the score of safety, the older design is the better one.
He was excused on the score of ill health.
The building is admired on the score of proportion rather than ornament.
The financing is settled; you needn't worry on that score.

entries.ipa: /ˌviz ə ˈvi/ · also /ˌvi zɑ ˈvi/ · no weak form — the French stress on the final syllable is kept, and the middle à is already as reduced as it gets
entries.complement: noun phrase; a gerund is possible but stiff (vis-à-vis raising the cap); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [clause] vis-à-vis [noun phrase] / Vis-à-vis [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Not a synonym for versus. Versus sets two things against each other; vis-à-vis positions one relative to the other without any implication of conflict. Against in relation to, it is shorter, more clearly comparative, and noticeably more self-conscious.
variants: vis-a-vis
vis à vis (the grave accent is optional in American text, the hyphens are standard; all three are pronounced the same)
entries.meaning: 1. In relation to, compared with — the dominant modern sense. 2. Concerning, with regard to. 3. Face to face with — the literal, now rare.
examples: The dollar has weakened vis-à-vis the euro.
Our costs are high vis-à-vis the rest of the industry.
Nobody has explained the university's position vis-à-vis the union.
I have questions vis-à-vis the payment schedule.
Vis-à-vis the hiring freeze, no exceptions are being granted.
He found himself vis-à-vis the one person he'd hoped to avoid.
The two delegations sat vis-à-vis one another at a table the length of the room.

entries.ipa: /wɪθ ˈrɛf(ə)rəns tu/ · weak /wəθ ˈrɛfrəns tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (with reference to what the drawings show); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: With reference to [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] with reference to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Interchangeable with in reference to, and marginally more common in American use. In technical writing it shades toward "measured against a stated baseline," which is where it overlaps with with respect to. As with the whole family, no s — with references to means something else.
entries.meaning: Opens a letter or a paragraph by naming the document being answered. 1. Naming the document, message, or matter being answered — the correspondence use, and the padded one. 2. Technical: measured, dimensioned, or set against a stated baseline, where it is not padding and no shorter phrase does the job; this is the sense that overlaps with respect to.
examples: With reference to your email of the eleventh, the parts are on back order.
With reference to the earlier complaint, the account has been credited.
He declined to comment with reference to the pending case.
The drawings are dimensioned with reference to the northeast corner of the slab.
Salaries are set with reference to a published pay band.
Elevations on the survey are given with reference to mean sea level.

entries.ipa: /wɪθ rɪˈɡɑrd tu/ · weak /wəθ rɪˈɡɑrd tə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (with regard to filing late — the to is a preposition, so ✗ with regard to file late is impossible); never a finite that-clause (✗ with regard to that the rent is late). A fused wh- or whether-nominal is grammatical but clumsy here — write as to whether the deal closes, not with regard to whether the deal closes, and see as to.
entries.pattern: With regard to [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] with regard to [noun phrase] / negated as without regard to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The singular is the rule: with regard to, in regard to, without regard to. With regards to and in regards to are errors. Regards with an s is the plural of the noun meaning "good wishes" — which is exactly why Best regards closes a letter and give her my regards is idiomatic, while with regards to your invoice is not. The single exception in the whole family is as regards, where regards is a verb, not a noun.
variants: in regard to
having regard to (legal and British)
as regards and regarding as one-word and two-word alternatives
entries.meaning: The most common of the long-form topic phrases, and the one whose plural error is most worth learning to avoid. 1. Concerning — the plain topic sense, and the padded one, which an editor will cut to about, to on, or to nothing. 2. Negated as without regard to — "ignoring," "leaving out of account." This is the form worth keeping: no single English word replaces it, and it is the standard phrasing in nondiscrimination clauses.
examples: With regard to the security deposit, we'll need photographs.
The manual says nothing with regard to remote work.
With regard to your second question, the answer is no.
She wrote a careful memo with regard to the licensing terms.
With regard to funding, the grant covers only the first year.
Applicants are ranked without regard to age or ZIP code.
He acted without regard to the consequences.
The formula applies without regard to how long the employee has been there.

entries.ipa: /wɪθ rɪˈspɛkt tu/ · weak /wəθ rɪˈspɛkt tə/
entries.register: formal; the default in legal, mathematical, and engineering prose
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (with respect to whether the clause survives closing); never a finite that-clause. In the technical sense (2) the object must be a noun phrase naming a variable or a baseline.
entries.pattern: [clause] with respect to [noun phrase] / With respect to [noun phrase], [clause] / abbreviated w.r.t. in technical notation
entries.contrast: With all due respect is a different animal entirely — a discourse hedge announcing that disagreement is coming, not a preposition of topic. And in respect of is the British counterpart of sense 1; American writers should stay with with respect to.
entries.meaning: 1. Concerning, as regards. 2. Technical: measured or varied against a stated variable or baseline.
examples: With respect to the third count, the jury could not agree.
The lease is silent with respect to subletting.
Company policy with respect to overtime changed in March.
Differentiate the function with respect to x.
The bracket's position is fixed with respect to the frame, not the wheel.
Returns are reported with respect to a benchmark index.

entries.ipa: /æz ə ˈmætər əv/ · weak /əz ə ˈmætər ə/
entries.register: formal; standard in legal, policy, and business prose
entries.complement: a bare abstract noun with no article — law, fact, policy, principle, right, course, practice, convenience. Nothing else goes here: no gerund, no concrete noun, and no clause of any kind (✗ as a matter of the policy, ✗ as a matter of that it was late).
entries.pattern: As a matter of [bare abstract noun], [clause] / [clause] as a matter of [bare abstract noun]
entries.contrast: The articles are the trap and they run in opposite directions: a is fixed before matter and nothing may stand before the noun after of — as a matter of policy, never ✗ as matter of policy and never ✗ as a matter of the policy. Two of the fixed phrases have drifted apart in meaning: as a matter of law still restricts a claim to one dimension and is the near twin of in point of law, while as a matter of fact has stopped restricting anything and now just means "actually," usually introducing a correction. Against in terms of, which names the units something is measured in, this phrase names the kind of consideration at work — legal, factual, principled, or merely habitual.
variants: as a matter of course (routinely, without a decision being made each time)
as a matter of fact (a discourse marker meaning "actually")
as a matter of law (a term of art: decided by the judge on the legal rule, not by the jury on the evidence)
entries.meaning: Says which order of consideration a statement belongs to. In American legal writing it is doing real work; everywhere else it is usually a way of sounding deliberate. 1. Restricting a claim to one order of consideration — legal, factual, or principled. 2. Naming a settled practice rather than a decision — as a matter of policy, as a matter of course. 3. As a matter of fact — no longer a restriction at all, but a corrective discourse marker.
examples: As a matter of law, the release bars every claim in the complaint.
He refused as a matter of principle, knowing it would cost him the contract.
The court reached the question as a matter of first impression.
The company does not comment on personnel decisions as a matter of policy.
Invoices over ten thousand dollars are reviewed twice as a matter of course.
Exit interviews are recorded as a matter of routine.
As a matter of fact, the inspection had already been scheduled.
She wasn't late; as a matter of fact she was the first one there.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.term: as far as X is concerned
entries.ipa: /æz ˈfɑr æz ... ɪz kənˈsɜrnd/ · weak /əz ˈfɑr əz ... ɪz kənˈsɜrnd/
entries.type: complex and discontinuous — a fossilized clause that works as a preposition, with its object sitting inside the frame rather than after it
entries.complement: a noun phrase or objective pronoun in the gap (as far as the wiring is concerned); the frame then closes with is/are concerned or goes/go. Never a finite that-clause inside the gap, and note the cross-class trap: as far as followed by a whole clause and no closing is concerned (as far as I know, as far as I can tell, as far as anyone remembers) is the conjunction, a different construction that hedges the speaker's certainty rather than restricting a domain.
entries.pattern: As far as [noun phrase] is concerned, [clause] / [clause], as far as [noun phrase] goes / As far as [pronoun] is concerned, [clause]
entries.contrast: Two different jobs hide in the same frame. With a person as the object it means "in that person's opinion" (as far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed); with a thing it means "within that domain" (as far as the wiring is concerned, the house is fine). Note that the verb agrees with the object: as far as the numbers are concerned.
variants: as far as X goes (more casual)
so far as X is concerned (formal and slightly British)
truncated as far as X (As far as money, we're fine) — very common in American speech and still flagged as nonstandard in edited prose
entries.meaning: Restricts a claim to one domain or one person's view, almost always implying that the picture changes outside it.
examples: As far as I'm concerned, the matter is closed.
As far as the wiring is concerned, the inspector found nothing wrong.
The car's fine as far as the engine goes — the body is another story.
As far as the numbers are concerned, we're ahead of last quarter.
As far as she was concerned, the apology had never happened.
As far as scheduling goes, Tuesday is the only day that works.

entries.ipa: /baɪ ˈweɪ əv/ · weak /baɪ ˈweɪ ə/
entries.complement: in sense 1 a bare abstract noun with no article (by way of apology) or a gerund (by way of explaining himself); in senses 2 and 3 an ordinary noun phrase. Never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [clause] by way of [noun phrase] / By way of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: In the sense that belongs to this file, the object is a bare abstract noun with no article: by way of apology, not by way of an apology. Put an article in and you have either the route sense or a mistake. The route sense (flew to Lisbon by way of Newark) belongs with the prepositions of path and is included below only so the two are not confused.
entries.meaning: 1. As a form of, in the character of, for the purpose of — a bare abstract noun follows. 2. Via, by the route of — spatial, and treated with the prepositions of path. 3. In the way of, as regards — chiefly in negative or quantified statements.
examples: By way of explanation, he pointed to the schedule on the wall.
She sent flowers by way of apology.
By way of introduction, let me say how the panel will run.
We drove to Santa Fe by way of Taos.
The shipment came by way of Rotterdam.
The prosecution offered little by way of physical evidence.
There isn't much by way of nightlife within thirty miles.

entries.ipa: /fɔr ˈpɜrpəsəz əv/ · weak /fɚ ˈpɜrpəsəz ə/ (for reduces to /fɚ/, also written /fər/, and final of to /ə/)
entries.register: formal and legal — the standard American drafting phrase for fencing off a definition
entries.complement: a noun phrase, most often naming a statute, section, rule, article, or analysis (for purposes of this Article, for purposes of the overtime calculation); a gerund is possible and common in tax drafting (for purposes of calculating basis); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: For purposes of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] for purposes of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The article and the number decide which phrase you have, and they are not interchangeable. For the purpose of + gerund states an aim and belongs with the prepositions of purpose — for the purpose of raising money — while for purposes of + a named text restricts a definition to one domain: for purposes of this section, "employee" includes a contractor. Writing for the purpose of this section is the usual slip, and it says something the drafter did not mean. Against in the case of, which subdivides a class of people or things, this phrase fences off a body of rules; against as a matter of, it limits where a definition applies rather than what kind of consideration is in play.
variants: for the purposes of (with the article — the British and Commonwealth drafting form, and still seen in older American statutes)
solely for purposes of (the emphatic drafting version)
entries.meaning: Declares that what follows is true inside one stated set of rules and nowhere else. It is how American drafters make a word mean something locally without disturbing its ordinary meaning. 1. Restricting a definition to a named text. 2. Restricting a computation or a test to one procedure.
examples: For purposes of this section, "resident" means anyone domiciled in the state.
The two subsidiaries are treated as one employer for purposes of the statute.
She is not a public figure for purposes of the defamation analysis.
Stock options are counted as wages for purposes of the overtime calculation.
For purposes of the audit, the fiscal year ends September 30.
For purposes of calculating seniority, unpaid leave does not count.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈkeɪs əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈkeɪs ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (in the case of subletting without notice), or a fused wh-nominal (in the case of who inherits); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: In the case of [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] in the case of [noun phrase] / except in the case of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The article changes the meaning completely, and this is the error to watch. In case of — no the — is contingency, an if: in case of fire, use the stairs, treated with in case of. In the case of singles out one member of a class already under discussion and says how the general rule lands on it: in the case of the Denver office, the lease runs another four years. Swapping them produces nonsense in both directions. Against as for, which switches topic conversationally and often with a sting, in the case of is analytic and neutral. Against as far as X is concerned, it subdivides a class rather than restricting a claim to a domain. Editors cut it whenever the sentence survives without it: in the case of older buildings, permits take longer is just older buildings take longer to permit.
entries.meaning: Picks one member out of a class and states how the general rule applies to it. The phrase earns its place when a real class is genuinely being subdivided, and it is padding the rest of the time.
examples: In the case of part-time employees, the waiting period is ninety days.
The deduction is capped at two thousand dollars, except in the case of farm equipment.
In the case of the Denver office, the lease runs another four years.
In the case of a tie, the chair votes.
Refunds are issued automatically, though not in the case of tickets bought through a reseller.
In the case of who inherits the house, the will is silent.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈpɔɪnt əv/ · weak /ɪn ˈpɔɪnt ə/
entries.register: formal, verging on archaic outside two fixed phrases
entries.complement: a bare abstract noun — fact, law, time, form, accuracy — with no article. No gerund, no clause, no ordinary concrete noun.
entries.pattern: In point of [bare abstract noun], [clause] / [clause] in point of [bare abstract noun]
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with a case in point (an illustrating example), to the point (relevant), or up to a point (partially) — same noun, unrelated idioms. In point of fact is a stuffier, more insistent actually, and like actually it is usually corrective: it announces that what follows contradicts what was just assumed.
entries.meaning: Restricts a statement to a single dimension. In modern American English it survives almost entirely in in point of fact and, in legal writing, in point of law. 1. In point of fact — a stuffier, more insistent actually, and nearly always corrective. 2. In point of law — restricting a claim to the legal dimension; compare as a matter of law, which is the commoner American phrasing. 3. Any other single dimension — archaic outside the two fixed phrases.
examples: In point of fact, the building was condemned two years earlier.
He was, in point of fact, never employed there at all.
The claim is unreviewable in point of law.
In point of law the two instruments are identical, whatever the parties intended.
In point of time, the second signature came first.
The two editions are identical in point of substance, if not of price.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ˈtɜrmz əv/ · weak /ɪn ˈtɜrmz ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or a fused wh-nominal (in terms of what it costs); never a finite that-clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in terms of [noun phrase] / In terms of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: The plural is fixed — in term of is an error. More importantly, two very different uses share the phrase, and only one survives editing. Sense 1 states the units or framework of a measurement and is precise. Sense 2 is a filler about, and it is the single most frequently cut phrase in American editing: in terms of the budget, we're fine is just the budget is fine.
entries.meaning: 1. Using the concepts, units, or framework of something stated — precise and defensible. 2. As regards, with respect to — extremely common in speech and almost always removable.
examples: Measured in terms of calories, the two meals are nearly identical.
He explained the whole conflict in terms of water rights.
The contract is priced in terms of barrels, not dollars.
In terms of the timeline, we're about two weeks behind.
She's strongest in terms of client work.
In terms of what it costs, nobody has given us a number.
In terms of the weather, Saturday looks better.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈweɪ əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈweɪ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund; never a clause of any kind. In sense 1 a quantity word (anything, much, little, nothing) almost always comes first.
entries.pattern: [quantity word: anything, much, little, nothing] in the way of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The topic sense almost always follows a quantifier, and usually a negative or a question — anything in the way of, little in the way of, nothing in the way of. Strip the quantifier and you get the literal blocking sense (standing in the way of the merger), which is a wholly different construction and the reason this idiom is slowly disappearing. By way of covers nearly the same ground in sense 3 and sounds less antique.
entries.meaning: 1. In the category of, as regards — after a word of quantity. 2. Literally blocking — a different construction, listed for contrast.
examples: Do you have anything in the way of vegetarian options?
The apartment offers very little in the way of storage.
He'd received nothing in the way of an explanation.
There isn't much in the way of competition in that market.
A parked truck stood in the way of the ambulance.
Nothing now stands in the way of the sale.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.ipa: /wɛn ɪt ˈkʌmz tu/ · weak /wən ɪt ˈkʌmz tə/ · the stress sits on comes; when and the final to both reduce, and in fast speech the whole frame runs together as /wənɪtˈkʌmztə/
entries.type: complex and fossilized from a clause — a when-clause that has hardened into a topic-marking preposition, and no longer names a time
entries.register: neutral to informal; extremely common in American speech, journalism, and advertising
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun (when it comes to me, never ✗ when it comes to I), gerund (when it comes to raising money), or a fused wh-nominal (when it comes to who actually decides); never a finite that-clause (✗ when it comes to that the rent is late). The to is a preposition, not the infinitive marker, which is exactly why a verb after it takes -ing: ✗ when it comes to raise money → when it comes to raising money.
entries.pattern: When it comes to [noun phrase], [clause] / [clause] when it comes to [noun phrase] / past: when it came to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The living American equivalent of as far as X is concerned, and much the commoner of the two in speech. It differs from as for in that it does not switch topics — it narrows to a domain inside the topic already running, and it very often sets up a contrast with what was just said: He's careless with money. When it comes to his tools, he's meticulous. Editors treat it as padding in formal prose exactly the way they treat in terms of, and the cure is the same: make the object the subject of the sentence. Cross-class test: the frame is a preposition only when a noun phrase follows to and no clause follows the frame's own verb; ordinary temporal when it comes to a vote we'll know — where a vote is an event on the clock — is the literal when-clause it grew out of.
variants: when it came to (past, and the only inflection the frame allows)
when it comes down to (adds "in the end, after everything else is stripped away")
if it comes to (hypothetical, and often a threat)
entries.meaning: Narrows the discussion to one domain, usually to say the general rule does not hold there. It is the workhorse of American conversational framing. 1. Restricting a claim to one domain. 2. Setting up a contrast with what was just said. 3. With a gerund, where the domain is an activity.
examples: When it comes to pricing, nobody in the region touches them.
The state is generous when it comes to unemployment benefits.
When it comes to who actually decides, the org chart tells you nothing.
She's fearless in a meeting. When it comes to small talk, she's hopeless.
He'll argue about anything. When it comes to apologizing, he goes quiet.
When it comes to raising money, he'd rather do anything else.
When it came to signing the lease, both of them found reasons to wait.
related: as far as X is concerned

entries.ipa: /æz/ · weak /əz/
entries.type: simple — the same word is also a subordinating conjunction of time and cause (as I was leaving), half of the comparative correlative as … as, and a relative pronoun after such and the same (such delays as we saw)
entries.complement: a noun phrase, bare (as chair, as treasurer) or with an article (as a nurse), with any pronoun in the objective case (cast as me, never ✗ as I). After verbs of classification it also takes an adjective phrase (regard the figure as unreliable, dismissed the claim as premature) and a participial phrase (described as having failed to file, counts as cheating). Never a finite clause — a clause after as means you have the conjunction, not the preposition — and never a bare gerund in the role sense: ✗ He works as driving a bus → He works as a bus driver.
entries.pattern: [verb] as [noun phrase] / As [noun phrase], [clause] / [verb] [object] as [noun phrase or adjective phrase], with verbs of classification: regard/see/describe/treat/define/cite/use/dismiss X as Y
entries.contrast: As versus like is the central rule. As your doctor, I'd advise against it means the speaker is the doctor; Like your doctor, I'd advise against it means the speaker is somebody else who happens to agree. In careful American English, as takes a role and like takes a resemblance. Two corollaries: such as introduces genuine members of a set (fruit such as pears) and informal like does the same job in speech; and like used as a conjunction (like I said, like I told you) is thoroughly established in American speech but still cut in edited prose, where the conjunction is as. Against for: mistaken for a doctor means misidentified, taken as a compliment means interpreted. Cross-class test — the object: She works as a nurse is the preposition (object a nurse, a noun phrase) against She works as I do (conjunction, whole clause); as tall as I am is the comparative correlative; and in such delays as we saw, as is a relative pronoun. Anything headed by as that is completed by a clause is the conjunction, and that includes the compounds as if, as though, as soon as, as long as, and as far as — none of them takes an object, and none of them may be stranded.
entries.meaning: The role preposition, and one of the highest-frequency words in English. Senses 1 through 5 are prepositional; sense 6 is the conjunction, included because learners constantly confuse it with the preposition. 1. The job, office, or role a person holds. 2. The function a thing is put to. 3. In the character of — costume, casting, or disguise. 4. At a stage of life, or in a stated condition. 5. The status a verb of classification assigns, after regard, see, describe, treat, define, count, cite, dismiss, know — the one sense that admits an adjective or a participle in place of a noun. 6. Not a preposition — the conjunction of time and cause, which takes a whole clause and governs no object.
examples: She spent eleven years as a public defender.
As treasurer, he signs every check over five thousand dollars.
He was hired as a consultant and stayed as head of the department.
We used a milk crate as a nightstand for most of that year.
The gym doubles as a storm shelter.
He came to the party as a bag of jelly beans.
She was cast as Lady Macbeth three seasons running.
As a child, she spent every summer on the lake.
As a young attorney he took whatever walked through the door.
The letter was dismissed as a hoax within a day.
Most economists regard the figure as unreliable.
He's known as the only person who can fix that machine.
Skipping the deposition would count as defaulting.
The lights went out as she reached the landing.
As the roads were closed, we stayed another night.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə kəˈpæsəti əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə kəˈpæsəti ə/
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a role, generally without an article; never a clause and never a gerund.
entries.pattern: in the capacity of [role] / in [possessive] capacity as [role] / acting in the capacity of [role]
entries.contrast: The two frames take different prepositions and mixing them is the usual error: the article-less version takes of (in the capacity of trustee), the possessive version takes as (in her capacity as trustee). In the capacity as is wrong. Against plain as, this phrase exists to insist that only one of a person's several roles is in play — which is precisely why lawyers use it.
variants: in one's capacity as (in her capacity as trustee) — much the commoner American form
acting in the capacity of
entries.meaning: Separates the hat from the person wearing it. It matters where someone holds more than one office and only one of them is acting.
examples: She signed in the capacity of executor, not in her personal capacity.
He attended in the capacity of an observer and asked no questions.
Statements made in his capacity as spokesman are attributable to the agency.
The auditor may not serve in the capacity of a director.
In her capacity as department chair, she controls the teaching schedule.
Any liability incurred in the capacity of agent falls on the principal.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈfɔrm əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈfɔrm ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (help in the form of forgiving two months' rent); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun] in the form of [noun phrase] / [clause] in the form of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The neutral member of the guise family and the one American writers actually need. In the guise of asserts that the appearance is a false front; in the form of only states the shape the thing turned out to have and passes no judgment — compare a tax increase in the guise of a user fee (an accusation) with relief in the form of a rent credit (a description). Against in the person of, which is reserved for human beings, in the form of covers things, and applying it to a person is faintly comic unless the comedy is intended. Against by way of sense 1, which names a purpose (flowers by way of apology), this phrase names a substance.
entries.meaning: Names the shape an abstraction turned out to have. The sentence introduces something general — help, pressure, evidence, a warning, compensation — and this phrase says what it concretely was.
examples: Relief arrived in the form of a federal grant.
The company offered compensation in the form of store credit.
Pressure came in the form of three letters from the state attorney general.
The only evidence is circumstantial, in the form of a parking receipt.
He got his answer in the form of a locked door.
Support was offered in the form of forgiving the first two months' rent.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈɡaɪz əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈɡaɪz ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (under the guise of protecting consumers); never a clause of any kind.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the guise of [noun phrase] / In the guise of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: In the form of is neutral and merely describes a shape; in the guise of is skeptical and asserts that the appearance is false. Against as, which takes the role at face value, this phrase always implies a disguise or a pretext — so a tax increase in the guise of a user fee is an accusation, not a description, and a writer who does not intend the accusation should use in the form of.
variants: under the guise of — the commoner form in American English by a wide margin and the more accusatory of the two; in the guise of keeps a faint literary and mythological flavor (the god in the guise of a swan), while under the guise of belongs to investigative journalism and litigation
under the pretext of, under cover of (the plainer synonyms)
entries.meaning: Assigns a role and disbelieves it in the same breath. 1. Wearing an assumed shape or identity — the literary and mythological use. 2. Presented as something more innocuous than it is — the accusation. 3. Under the guise of — the commoner American form, and the more openly accusatory; it takes a gerund far more readily than in the guise of does.
examples: The god appears in the guise of an old woman at the crossroads.
He turned up at the border in the guise of a relief worker.
The bill arrived in the guise of a routine reauthorization.
It's censorship in the guise of quality control.
They cut the program in the guise of streamlining.
The surveillance ran for years under the guise of routine maintenance.
She got into the building under the guise of delivering flowers.
The fee was raised under the guise of covering administrative costs.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈpɜrsən əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈpɜrsən ə/
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, usually a name or a title; never a clause.
entries.pattern: [abstract noun or clause] in the person of [name]
entries.contrast: In the form of does the same job for things (help arrived in the form of a tow truck); in the person of is reserved for human beings and is faintly grand. It names the individual who embodies something abstract that the sentence has just introduced — the structure is always "X arrived, and X turned out to be this specific person."
entries.meaning: Identifies the human being in whom an abstraction shows up.
examples: Relief arrived in the person of a retired paramedic who lived two doors down.
The opposition found a leader in the person of a thirty-year-old schoolteacher.
The company's institutional memory survives in the person of one payroll clerk.
Authority was present in the person of the deputy commissioner.
He met his match in the person of his own daughter.

entries.ipa: /ɪn ðə ˈroʊl əv/ · weak /ɪn ðə ˈroʊl ə/
entries.complement: a noun phrase, usually with an article or a proper name; never a clause.
entries.pattern: [clause] in the role of [noun phrase] / In the role of [noun phrase], [clause]
entries.contrast: Theatrical by default — in a cast list it is the standard formula — and extended from there to any adopted function. Outside casting, plain as is shorter and nearly always better: she acted as mediator beats she acted in the role of mediator. Against in the capacity of, this phrase is descriptive where that one is jurisdictional.
entries.meaning: Names the part somebody is playing, on a stage or off one.
examples: In the role of Willy Loman, an understudy nobody had heard of.
She found herself in the role of referee between two departments.
He was miscast in the role of the reasonable one.
The agency acts in the role of clearinghouse for the whole region.
In the role of narrator, the older brother is not to be trusted.

entries.ipa: /kweɪ/ · also /kwɑ/ · no weak form — it is always stressed, being the pivot of the construction it appears in
entries.type: simple (Latin, ablative feminine of quī "who, which")
entries.register: formal and academic — philosophy, law, and theory
entries.complement: a bare noun phrase, characteristically without an article and very often repeating the noun it follows (the state qua state). Never a clause, never a gerund.
entries.pattern: [noun] qua [noun] / [clause] qua [noun]
entries.contrast: Qua means "in the capacity of, considered strictly as, in that thing's character of" and its job is to isolate one aspect of a thing from its other aspects. As would serve most readers just as well; qua signals a technical register and a deliberate act of analytical separation. Note the pronunciation: /kweɪ/ is the established English form and the spelling-based /kwɑ/ is also heard, but it is never /kwɔ/, and qua is not related to the qua- of quality or the quo of status quo.
entries.meaning: The philosopher's preposition. It splits a thing from itself so that only one of its roles is on the table.
examples: The university qua employer has obligations it does not have qua educator.
He is studying the novel qua commodity, not qua art.
The state qua state cannot hold a religious belief.
What interests her is the building qua structure, not qua landmark.
A judge qua judge has no opinions, which is a useful fiction.

entries.ipa: /ˈʌndər ˈkʌlər əv/ · weak /ˈʌndɚ ˈkʌlɚ ə/
entries.register: legal — a term of art in American civil-rights and criminal practice, and rare outside it
entries.complement: a bare noun phrase naming an authority, office, or body of law, with no article: color of law, color of state law, color of office, color of authority. A gerund is not idiomatic, and no clause of any kind is possible.
entries.pattern: [verb] under color of [bare noun phrase] / acting under color of [bare noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The legal sibling of under the guise of. Both say a role is being used as cover, but they are not interchangeable: under the guise of is a journalist's accusation of pretext, while under color of is a jurisdictional test — an officer acts under color of law whenever the act was made possible by the office, authorized or not, which is precisely why the phrase does not mean "lawfully." Against plain as and in the capacity of, which take the office at face value, this phrase says the office was the instrument. Note the vocabulary trap: color here is the old legal sense "appearance, semblance, pretense," unrelated to the everyday noun — and the American spelling has no u, in this phrase as everywhere else.
variants: under color of law — the fixed statutory phrase of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and 18 U.S.C. § 242, and the form nearly every occurrence takes
under color of office
under color of authority
the related adjective colorable (a colorable claim), which means "plausible enough to argue," not "false"
entries.meaning: Names the official authority that made a wrongful act possible. It is the hinge on which American civil-rights liability turns, which is why it is worth knowing that it describes a source of power rather than a lawful exercise of it. 1. The statutory test — conduct made possible by public office. 2. Abuse of a particular office, outside the § 1983 formula.
examples: The suit alleges that the deputies acted under color of state law.
Section 1983 reaches only conduct under color of law.
A private security guard is not ordinarily acting under color of state authority.
He collected the fees under color of office and kept them.
The indictment charges deprivation of rights under color of law.
Evictions carried out under color of a forged court order are void.

entries.ipa: /ˈpeɪsi/ · also /ˈpɑtʃeɪ/, /ˈpɑkeɪ/ · no weak form — it is a two-syllable Latin word carrying its own stress, and it never reduces to the /peɪs/ of the English noun
entries.complement: a personal name, or a noun phrase naming a person or an authority. Never a clause, never a gerund, never an abstract topic.
entries.pattern: Pace [name], [clause] / [clause] (pace [name])
entries.contrast: A homograph, not a sense, of the everyday noun and verb pace /peɪs/ meaning "step" — different word, different origin, different pronunciation. And it is emphatically not a synonym for according to; it means close to the opposite: "with apologies to X, who argues otherwise." Writers who use it as according to invert their own sentence.
entries.meaning: Concedes, politely and in passing, that a named authority disagrees with what you are about to say.
examples: Pace Freud, the dream literature has moved on considerably.
The manuscript is, pace Robertson, almost certainly a later copy.
Pace my colleagues in the department, the reform did work.
Attendance has risen every year (pace the recent editorials).
Pace Aristotle, not every polity aims at the good.

entries.ipa: /ˈspikɪŋ əv/ · weak /ˈspikɪŋ ə/
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund, or the fused relative which (speaking of which); never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: Speaking of [noun phrase], [clause] / Speaking of which, [clause] — essentially always sentence-initial
entries.contrast: It is a topic-shift device, not a framing preposition: it claims that the object was just mentioned and uses that mention as a bridge to something new. As for also shifts topic, but it returns to one item out of a set already under discussion rather than following an association. By origin this is a dangling participle — nobody is doing the speaking — but it has grammaticalized completely, and no usage authority requires a matching subject.
variants: talking of (chiefly British)
speaking of which (fixed)
which reminds me (the non-prepositional equivalent)
entries.meaning: The conversational hinge. It licenses a change of subject by pretending the change was inevitable.
examples: Speaking of the weather, did you ever get the gutters cleaned?
Speaking of which, your brother called twice.
Speaking of people who never answer email — has anyone heard from Dana?
She's in Denver now. Speaking of Denver, the flights are absurd.
Speaking of being late, we should probably leave.
Speaking of money, the deposit hasn't cleared.
